draft.title: Rites of passage
card: A rite of passage is a ceremony or ritual that marks a change in a person's status in a group or society. The person is treated differently afterwards.
Common examples are a bar or bat mitzvah, a school graduation and a wedding. Each one publicly marks a move to a new status.
Rites of passage are shared with others, such as family, a community or a school. The group recognises the new status, and it often expects new roles or responsibilities.
Different cultures and groups hold different rites, and a rite can mark a change at any point in life, not only the move to adulthood.
draft.remember: A rite of passage is a ceremony that publicly marks a change in status.

a.q: Which of these is the best example of a rite of passage?
opts: A graduation ceremony at the end of Year 12
A student deciding to study harder this term
A teenager getting a part-time job on her own
A family moving to a new suburb in the city
a.why: A graduation is a ceremony where a group publicly recognises a new status. The part-time job may bring new responsibility, but it is not a ceremony that marks a change in status.
a.clue: Look for a ceremony that a group holds to mark a change.

b.q: Tariq turns 13 and has a bar mitzvah at his synagogue in Sydney, with family and community watching. Why is this a rite of passage?
opts: It publicly marks his change in status in the community
It shows he has gained full independence from his family
It happens because he has turned a certain age in years
It is a celebration that only his close family attends
b.why: The ceremony is shared with the community, which recognises Tariq's new status. Age alone is not the reason: a birthday party at 13 would not be a rite of passage without a ceremony marking a change in status.
b.clue: Think about what the ceremony does, not just when it happens.

a.best: A graduation ceremony at the end of Year 12

b.best: It publicly marks his change in status in the community

proposal.title: Rites of passage
card: A rite of passage is a ceremony or ritual that marks a change in a person's status in a group or society. The person is treated differently afterwards.
Common examples are a bar or bat mitzvah, a school graduation and a wedding. Each one publicly marks a move to a new status.
Rites of passage are shared with others, such as family, a community or a school. The group recognises the new status, and it often expects new roles or responsibilities.
Different cultures hold different rites, and they can mark a change at any point in life. What makes an event a rite is the shared marking of a new status, not a date or age alone.
proposal.remember: An event becomes a rite of passage when a group marks and recognises a new status.

a.q: Which of these events is a rite of passage?
opts: A wedding where a couple marry in front of their families
A yearly birthday dinner held with close family
A school swimming carnival held every summer
A family reunion held each year at Christmas
a.why: After a wedding, the couple has a new status as a married couple, and their families recognise it. The birthday dinner is shared with family too, but a yearly dinner does not leave anyone with a new status.
a.clue: After which event does someone hold a new status?

It is a celebration that only his close family attends
b.why: The ceremony is shared with the community, which recognises Tariq's new status. Age alone is not the reason: a birthday party at 13 would not be a rite of passage without a shared marking of a new status.
b.clue: Think about what the ceremony does, not just when it happens.

b.best: It publicly marks his change in status in the community
